newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algeria sees debt bonus of $16 bln over four years.
newsitem.headline: Algeria sees debt bonus of $16 bln over four years.

text.p: Algeria will have "exceptional finance" totalling $16 billion over four years until 1998 from rescheduling around $12 billion of its foreign debts, according to a report from the Algerian presidency obtained by Reuters.

The report, the basis of debate on the economy in Algiers last week, said that rescheduling had brought the debt/service ratio down to 32.7 percent in 1996 from 100 percent of foreign income in the first quarter of 1994.
But it warned that the ratio would climb to 47.1 percent in 1998 under the impact of repaying credits to the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
"At the same time, the total outstanding debt bill will drop relative to exports, to 267 percent in 1999 against 316 percent in 1994," the report said.
The report did not say how this $16 billion bonus would be achieved, but besides easing debt repayments, the rescheduling released further loans, including an IMF one of $1.4 billion.
Algeria, an OPEC member, ran up foreign debt estimated at $32 billion over years of centralised state control of the economy, despite its oil and gas wealth.
It resisted rescheduling until it stood on the brink of bankruptcy in 1994 when oil prices fell and its earnings slumped to $8.4 billion and debt servicing stood at $9 billion.
The country spends an estimated $2.5 billion on importing essential foods for its 29 million people.

According to the presidency report, entitled "The Algerian Economy, medium-term challenges and choice (1996-2000)", Algeria's income from oil exports between 1996 to 1999 should total between $41.2 billion and $44.8 billion.

The estimates were based on forecasts of $15 or $17 a barrel. Algeria has an OPEC quota of 750,000 barrels per day (bpd). The latest Reuters survey, on Monday, put its wellhead flow in September at 830,000 bpd.
Energy exports through state-owned Sonatrach earn Algeria over 95 percent of its foreign income and Algiers has forecast oil output will reach one million bpd in the year 2000.
Traditionally cautious in its forecasts, Algeria estimated income for 1995 on an average price of $16.27 per barrel, while actual income was $17.9 a barrel.
In the first half of 1996, average income was $22 a barrel, against estimates in its 1996 calendar year budget of $16.5.

Last week's debate focused on how to salvage non-energy industry, and the report said: "The annual growth target of around five percent must...be supported by real industrial and production policies to give a base for the rehabilitation of public enterprises and stimulate national production."
Unemployment and poverty have long been blamed by officials for providing ready recruits for Moslem fundamentalists seeking for the past five years to overthrow the authorities.
Some 400, heavily-subsidised state firms outside the energy sector employ about 1.7 million people. But most operate at only 35 percent capacity.
One Western diplomat commented: "They are acting as a sort of welfare system to keep people off the streets and out of the hands of the Islamists."
The presidency report said 100,000 people joined the ranks of the jobless in 1995, to lift the total to 1.76 million or 25 percent of the workforce against 24.36 percent in 1994.
